p: Suniti Devi was born on 30 September 1864, a daughter of Keshub Chandra Sen of Calcutta and Jagonmohini Sen. She was fourteen when she married. For two years afterwards she stayed in her father's house, since her husband left for London for higher studies immediately after the wedding. She had four sons and three daughters. Two of her sons, Rajendra Narayan and Jitendra Narayan, later became Maharajas of Cooch Behar. Her daughters Sudhira and Pratibha married the brothers Alan and Miles Mander of Wightwick Manor in England, and Sukriti married Jyotsna Nath Ghoshal, a nephew of Rabindranath Tagore.

In 1887, when she attended the Golden Jubilee of Queen Victoria with her husband, she was made a Companion of the Order of the Crown of India, the first Indian woman to receive the honour. She was also present at the Delhi Durbar of 1911.

The girls' school that her husband set up in her name in 1881, later called Suniti Academy, was her idea. She gave it annual grants, exempted the pupils from tuition fees and rewarded those who did well. She arranged for palace cars to carry the girls between home and school and, to avoid controversy, ordered the car windows to be curtained. With her sister Sucharu Devi, Maharani of Mayurbhanj, she financed the foundation of the Maharani Girls' High School in Darjeeling in 1908. She was President of the State Council and in 1932 the first President of the All Bengal Women's Union.

She was also an author. Bengal Dacoits and Tigers, a collection of short stories, was published in Calcutta in 1916. The Beautiful Mogul Princesses, published in London in 1918, tells the lives of Mumtaz Mahal, Zebunissa, Nur Jahan and another princess. The Autobiography of an Indian Princess appeared in London in 1921, and her last book, The Life of Princess Yashodara: Wife and Disciple of the Lord Buddha, in 1929. She died suddenly at Ranchi on 10 November 1932. In Cooch Behar the school, Sunity Road and a tank known as the Sunity Tank or Bairagi Dighi are named after her.

notes: The article expands CIE as 'Companion of the Order of the Crown of India' and dates it to the Golden Jubilee of 1887; it also says she attended 'the Diamond Jubilee celebrations of Queen Victoria in 1898' (the jubilee year looks wrong), which I left out.
Her books are told under 'Death and legacy' for want of a better heading among the three.
The Autobiography (1921) appears only in the article's External links.
The fourth princess of The Beautiful Mogul Princesses is named 'Reba' in the article; not a name I could place, so 'another princess'.
Ghoshal is 'the eldest son of Swarnakumari Devi (Rabindranath Tagore's sister)', hence 'nephew'.
